lessons.title: Logarithms and their laws
lessons.summary: Interpret a logarithm as an exponent, apply the laws and check the permitted bases and arguments.
lessons.objective: Evaluate logarithms exactly, combine terms of one base and determine the full domain.
lessons.before: Recall negative and fractional indices, including \(b^{-1}=\frac1b\) for \(b>0\).
lessons.ideas:
The statement \(\log_b y=x\) means \(b^x=y\), with \(b>0,\ b\ne1,\ y>0\).

For positive arguments the logarithm of a product is a sum. The logarithm of a quotient is a difference. A power of a positive argument gives a multiple of its logarithm.

A combined argument may be positive outside the original domain. Keep each original positive-argument restriction.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the common base and write all original restrictions.
  2. Apply the product, quotient or power law that matches the structure.
  3. Evaluate by rewriting a known number as a power.
mistakes: A real logarithm needs a positive argument.
Keep all original argument restrictions when combining logarithms.
The logarithm of a sum does not split into two logarithms.

examples.title: Use the power law
examples.question: Write \(\log_{7} \left(t^3\right)\) in terms of \(\log_{7} t\) for \(t>0\).
examples.solution: The exponent becomes a multiplier, so the expression is \(3\log_{7} t\).

lessons.title: Logarithmic equations
lessons.summary: Solve logarithmic equations and retain only the roots allowed by the original arguments.
lessons.objective: Solve equations by rewriting as indices, combining logarithms or substituting a logarithm as the variable.
lessons.before: Be ready to solve linear and quadratic equations and interpret a domain as a set.
lessons.ideas:
Before transforming the equation, require every original argument to be positive.

A single logarithm may be undone by exponentiating in its base.

A quadratic in \(\log_{b} x\) can be solved in that variable. Convert each admissible answer back to \(x\).
lessons.method:
1. Write the full domain.
  2. Combine matching bases or substitute for a repeated logarithm.
  3. Solve the simpler algebraic equation, convert back where necessary and check each candidate.
mistakes: A positive combined argument need not make each original argument positive.
A logarithm itself may be negative.
After a substitution, report values of the original variable.

examples.title: Convert to an index equation
examples.question: Solve \(\log_{4} \left(3x-2\right)=-1\).
examples.solution: The argument is \(3x-2=\frac{1}{4}\). Therefore \(x=\frac{3}{4}\) and the argument is positive.

examples.title: Keep the allowed product root
examples.question: Solve \(\log_{2} \left(x-3\right)+\log_{2} \left(x+4\right)=3\).
examples.solution: The domain is \(x>3\). Then \((x-3)(x+4)=8\) gives \(x^2+x-20=0\), with \(x=4\) or \(x=-5\). Keep \(x=4\).

examples.title: Return from the substitution
examples.question: The values of \(\log_{3} x\) are \(-2\) and \(1\). Find \(x\).
examples.solution: Exponentiate each value in base \(3\). The answers are \(3^{-2}=\frac{1}{9}\) and \(3^1=3\).

lessons.title: Exponential equations and inequalities
lessons.summary: Choose a common base or take logarithms and handle the direction of inequalities.
lessons.objective: Solve equations with unknown indices and inequalities with increasing or decreasing exponential functions.
lessons.before: Recall that equal powers of a fixed base greater than zero and different from one have equal exponents.
lessons.ideas:
When the expressions have a common base, compare their indices.

Taking the same logarithm on both sides converts a power into a factor multiplying its index.

For \(0
lessons.method:
1. Use a common base when possible, or isolate the power and take logarithms.
  2. Preserve positivity if you substitute for an exponential.
  3. Solve for the original variable and preserve strict endpoints.
mistakes: Check whether an equivalent inequality has a negative coefficient.
A substituted exponential is strictly positive.
Round only the final result when asked for a decimal answer.

examples.title: Choose a common base
examples.question: Solve \(16^{x-1}=8^{x+2}\).
examples.solution: Express both as powers of \(2\). Then \(4(x-1)=3(x+2)\), so \(x=10\).

examples.title: Take the same logarithm on each side
examples.question: Solve \(3^{2x}=14\) exactly.

examples.title: Reverse the order for decay
examples.question: Solve \(\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{x+1}>\frac1{16}\).
examples.solution: The right side is \(\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}\). Since the base is less than one, \(x+1<2\), so \(x<1\).

lessons.title: Natural logarithms and exponentials
lessons.summary: Use the inverse functions \(e^x\) and \(\ln x\) in equations, inequalities and graphs.
lessons.objective: Identify inverse domains and ranges, compare exponential growth and decay, and solve equations or inequalities using natural logarithms.
lessons.before: Recall that an inverse function exchanges the input and output.
lessons.ideas:
\(\ln(e^x)=x\) for every real \(x\) and \(e^{\ln x}=x\) for \(x>0\).

The graph of \(y=e^{kx}\) passes through \((0,1)\). It increases when \(k>0\) and decreases when \(k<0\).

On positive arguments, \(\ln x\) is increasing. Its input is \(1\) when its output is zero.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the inverse operation.
  2. Isolate the exponential or logarithm before applying the inverse.
  3. Keep the original positive-argument conditions.
mistakes: Check any restrictions before combining natural logarithms.
An exponential approaching zero remains positive.

examples.title: Undo the logarithm
examples.question: Simplify \(e^{\ln 7}\).
examples.solution: The exponential inverts the natural logarithm, giving \(7\).

examples.title: Solve using natural logarithms
examples.question: Solve \(4e^{2t}=11\) exactly.
examples.solution: Divide by \(4\) and take natural logarithms. Then \(t=\frac{\ln \left(\frac{11}{4}\right)}{2}\).

lessons.title: Linearising power and exponential models
lessons.summary: Choose log-log or log-linear axes, then recover model constants from the straight line.
lessons.objective: Use logarithms to linearise power and exponential models, and interpret the gradient, intercept and plotting domain.
lessons.before: Recall the meaning of gradient and vertical intercept, including when the plotted variables are transformed.
lessons.ideas:
\(y=Ax^n\) on positive inputs and outputs gives \(\ln y=\ln A+n\ln x\).

\(y=Ab^x\) with \(A,b>0\) gives \(\ln y=\ln A+x\ln b\). For \(y=Ae^{kx}\), the gradient of \(\ln y\) against \(x\) is \(k\).

Undo the logarithm on the vertical intercept to find the multiplier. Use the same base throughout one plot.
lessons.method:
1. Identify a power or exponential model.
  2. Define the plotted variables and take logarithms.
  3. Find the line’s gradient and intercept and convert back to the model constants.
mistakes: Do not take logs of already transformed data.
For a power model the gradient is the index, with no exponential conversion.
The intercept of the transformed graph is not the multiplier itself.

examples.title: Read a log-log plot
examples.question: A straight line has equation \(\log_{10}y=2\log_{10}x+1\). Recover the power model.
examples.solution: The power is \(2\) and the multiplier is \(10^1=10\). The model is \(y=10x^2\).

examples.title: Read a base from the gradient
examples.question: A plot satisfies \(\log_{10}y=3-x\). Find the multiplier and the base of the exponential model.
examples.solution: The multiplier is \(10^3=1000\) and the base is \(10^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}\).

examples.title: Use a natural-log plot
examples.question: A plot of \(\ln y\) against \(x\) has intercept \(\ln 8\) and gradient \(-\frac{3}{5}\). Find the model.
examples.solution: The multiplier is \(8\) and the gradient is the exponential rate. Hence \(y=8e^{-\frac{3}{5}x}\).

questions.title: Solve a quadratic in the logarithm
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(\left(\log_{5} x\right)^2-1 \log_{5} x-2=0\) for \(x>0\). Give both roots.
questions.solution_html:

Use \(x=5^{u}\) for each root. Both resulting \(x\)-values are positive.

questions.title: Determine a logarithm base
questions.prompt_html:
1. Given \(\log_{a} 16=4\), find the base \(a\). [2]
  2. Using this base, evaluate \(\log_{a} \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)+\log_{a} \sqrt{2}\) exactly. [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. The index form is \(a^4=16\). A logarithm base is positive and is different from \(1\), so \(a=2\).

questions.title: Use the original domain to select a root
questions.prompt_html:
For \(G(x)=\log_{2} \left(x-1\right)+\log_{2} \left(x+2\right)\), consider the following.

  1. Give the domain of \(G\). [1]
  2. Solve \(G(x)=2\). [3]
  3. Solve \(G(x)=3\). Give the answer exactly. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. The original conditions are \(x>1\) and \(x>-2\), so their intersection is \(x>1\).

  2. The product law gives \(\left(x-1\right)\left(x+2\right)=4\). Hence \(x^2+x-6=0\), giving \(x=-3\) or \(x=2\). Reject \(x=-3\) on the original domain.

  3. With right-hand side \(3\), the product must be \(8\). Now \(x^2+x-10=0\).

    The quadratic formula gives \(x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{41}}{2}\). Only the positive branch lies in \(x>1\).
questions.hint_html: The domain stays the same when the right-hand side changes.

questions.title: Read a logarithmic quotient
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(\log_{3} \left(2x+5\right)-\log_{3} \left(x-1\right)=1\). [3]
  2. Explain why \(\log_{3} \left(2x+5\right)-\log_{3} \left(x-1\right)=0\) has no real solution. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(x=8\)
  2. The sole algebraic candidate is outside the original domain.
questions.solution_html:
1. Both arguments are positive when \(x>1\). Combining the logarithms and exponentiating gives \(\frac{2x+5}{x-1}=3\). Thus \(2x+5=3x-3\), giving \(x=8\), which lies in the domain.

  2. Setting the quotient to \(1\) gives \(2x+5=x-1\) and hence \(x=-6\). This violates \(x>1\), so the original equation has no solution.
questions.hint_html: Convert each equation to one involving the ratio of the arguments.

questions.title: Find the repeated solution
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(H(x)=\left(\log_{4} x\right)^2-\log_{4} x\) for \(x>0\).

  1. Solve \(H(x)=2\) exactly. [3]
  2. Find the value of \(c\) for which \(H(x)=c\) has just one real solution in \(x>0\). Give that solution exactly. [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. Set \(u=\log_{4} x\). Then \(u^2-u-2=0\), with roots \(u=-1\) and \(u=2\). Undo the logarithm to get \(x=\frac{1}{4}\) and \(x=16\).

  2. Every real \(u\) gives one positive \(x\) through \(x=4^u\). Therefore a single \(x\) corresponds to a repeated \(u\).

    The expression \(u^2-u=\left(u-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-\frac{1}{4}\) takes its minimum once, at \(u=\frac{1}{2}\). This gives \(c=-\frac{1}{4}\) and \(x=2\).
questions.hint_html: A real value of the logarithm determines precisely one positive value of its argument.

questions.title: When does a hatchery pass a threshold?
questions.prompt_html:
A hatchery predicts \(N=34(1.25)^t\) larvae after \(t\) days, where \(t\ge0\).

  1. Find the time when the model first predicts \(90\) larvae. Give the time to 3 decimal places. [3]
  2. Find the least whole number of days after which the predicted count is strictly above \(90\). [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. Set \(34(1.25)^t=90\) and divide by \(34\).\[t=\frac{\log_{10} \left(\frac{90}{34}\right)}{\log_{10} 1.25}\approx 4.362\]

  2. Since \(1.25>1\), the predicted count increases. The inequality is \(t>\frac{\log_{10} \left(\frac{90}{34}\right)}{\log_{10} 1.25}\). The next whole number of days is \(5\).

questions.title: Decay and a strict limit

  2. The model is decreasing, so the concentration is below the limit for times strictly greater than the crossing time. The first whole-hour reading below the limit is at \(5\) hours.

questions.title: Find a transformed inverse
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=\ln(x-2)+3\).

  1. Find the domain and range of \(f\). [2]
  2. Find the inverse function and give its domain. [3]
  3. State the image under reflection in \(y=x\) of the point \((2+e,4)\) on the graph of \(f\). [1]
questions.solution_html:
1. The argument requires \(x-2>0\). On that domain, \(\ln(x-2)\) has every real output, as does its translation by \(3\).

  2. Set \(y=\ln(x-2)+3\). Then \(e^{y-3}=x-2\), so \(x=2+e^{y-3}\). The domain of the inverse is the range of \(f\), namely \(\mathbb R\).

  3. Reflection in \(y=x\) interchanges the coordinates. The image is \((4,2+e)\).
questions.hint_html: When undoing a function, undo the final vertical shift first.

questions.solution_html:

questions.title: Distinguish two proposed models
questions.prompt_html:
A process gives measurements \((x,y)=(1,3),\ (2,6),\ (4,24)\). Two models are proposed, \(y=Ax^n\) and \(y=Cb^x\), with \(A,C,b>0\).

  1. Determine both candidate models using the first two observations. [4]
  2. Decide which model agrees with the third observation. [2]
  3. State a choice of axes for a straight-line plot of the model that agrees. [1]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(y=3x\) and \(y=\frac{3}{2}\cdot2^x\)
  2. Only the exponential model agrees with the third observation.
  3. \(\ln y\) against \(x\)
questions.solution_html:
1. For the power model, at \(x=1\) the output gives \(A=3\). At \(x=2\), \(3\cdot2^n=6\), so \(n=1\).

    For the exponential model, the ratio of the second output to the first gives \(b=\frac{6}{3}=2\). From \(Cb=3\) obtain \(C=\frac{3}{2}\).

  2. At \(x=4\) the power model gives \(12\). The exponential model gives \(\frac{3}{2}\cdot2^4=24\), agreeing with the measurement.

  3. Plot \(\ln y\) vertically against \(x\) horizontally. The logarithm of the exponential model has gradient \(\ln 2\) and intercept \(\ln \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\).
questions.hint_html: Fit the first two observations in each model, then use the third observation to test the fit.
